course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The American Revolution
lesson.summary: How the war began, the turning points that saved the Patriot cause, and why Britain's apparent advantages were not enough to defeat the colonies.
learningGoals: Describe how the Revolutionary War began and widened from 1775 to 1778.
Identify the turning points that led to American victory.
Explain how militias, the Continental Army, Washington's leadership, ideological commitment, and European allies contributed to victory.
lesson.bigIdea: Despite loyalist opposition and Britain's apparent military and financial advantages, the Patriot cause succeeded because of the combined effects of the colonists' own efforts and help from abroad.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how various factors contributed to the American victory. Be ready to rank the factors and to say why a single cause is not enough.

sections.title: The war begins

blocks.text: Fighting began in April 1775 when British troops marching to seize colonial military supplies clashed with militia at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts. The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia, created the Continental Army, and named George Washington its commander. In July 1775 Congress sent the Olive Branch Petition to the king, who rejected it, and in July 1776 Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence.

Not all colonists supported the Patriot cause. Loyalists, who stayed faithful to the Crown, were a substantial minority, and some regions, especially in the South and in parts of New York, were bitterly divided. The war was in part a civil war among colonists.

sections.takeaway: The war began in Massachusetts in 1775, widened into a fight for independence by 1776, and divided colonists into Patriots and Loyalists.

sections.title: Turning points

blocks.text: After early defeats in 1776, Washington's surprise victory at Trenton at the end of the year lifted Patriot morale. The Patriot victory at Saratoga in New York in 1777 convinced France that the Americans could win. In 1778 France signed an alliance with the United States, and soon provided money, supplies, troops, and naval power. Spain and the Netherlands later joined the war against Britain, which turned the conflict into a wider European and global war.

The Continental Army endured the hard winter at Valley Forge in 1777–1778 and emerged better trained. After 1778 the British shifted their effort to the South, but they struggled to hold territory there. In 1781, a combined American and French army and French fleet trapped a British army under General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, and he surrendered in October. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence and set the new nation's boundaries from the Atlantic to the Mississippi River.

sections.takeaway: Saratoga brought the French alliance, and the allied victory at Yorktown led to the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

sections.title: Why the Patriots won

blocks.text: The Patriot cause succeeded because of the actions of colonial militias and the Continental Army, George Washington's military leadership, the colonists' ideological commitment and resilience, and assistance sent by European allies. Washington kept the army together through defeat and hardship and avoided the destruction of his forces. Militias controlled their local areas and wore down British forces. Many Patriots remained committed to republican ideals even when the war went badly.

Britain faced its own problems. Its armies were thousands of miles from home, the colonies were too large to occupy, and British leaders could not win the support of enough colonists to hold the territory that their soldiers captured. French assistance, in money, equipment, soldiers, and sea power, was decisive at Yorktown.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Do not credit one cause alone. The French alliance mattered, but it came after Saratoga showed that the Patriots could fight, and it did not remove the need for Washington's army or local militias.

sections.takeaway: Colonial effort, leadership, commitment, and European help together overcame Britain's advantages.

connections.title: The war's effects on society
connections.body: The war reached into every part of society. Topic 3.6 follows what it did to ideas about slavery, women, and politics.
connections.transferQuestion: Which two factors from this topic would you rank as most important in the Patriot victory, and why?
connections.feedback: A strong answer names two factors, supports each with a specific event, and explains why the others were less decisive.
